ch5.u1.definition: In 1665 Robert Hooke cut a thin slice of cork, put it under his own microscope, and saw it was built of tiny empty boxes. He called them cells, after the small rooms monks lived in. What he was looking at was dead: only the walls were left. It took another 170 years for anyone to say that every living thing is made this way.
a.ch5-u1-read-1.title: Cork, and the first cell
ch5.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: Hooke looked at cork and saw empty boxes. What was missing?
ch5.u1.quiz.q0.f0: They are empty now, but they were not always.
ch5.u1.quiz.q0.o1: Everything that had been alive inside them
ch5.u1.quiz.q0.f1: Right. Cork is dead bark. The walls survive and the living contents are long gone.
ch5.u1.quiz.q0.f2: The walls are the part he could see.
ch5.u1.quiz.q0.f3: His microscope was good enough. The cells really were empty.
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: Why does it matter that all living things are made of cells?
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.o0: It makes them easier to draw
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.o1: It means one explanation covers every living thing
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.f1: Right. A rule that holds for an onion and for you is worth far more than two separate rules.
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.o2: It proves living things are simple
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.f2: Cells are not simple. A single one runs hundreds of reactions at once.
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.o3: It explains why organisms are small
ch5.u1.quiz.q1.f3: Organisms are not small. Cells are, which is a different claim.
a.ch5-u1-quiz-2.title: What Hooke actually saw
ch5.plant.wall.label: Cell wall
ch5.plant.wall.do: Start with a rounded rectangle, drawn thick. This is the outer boundary.
ch5.plant.wall.does: A stiff jacket of cellulose outside the membrane. It stops the cell bursting when water rushes in, and it is why a plant stands up without any bones.
ch5.plant.wall.only: Plant cells only. An animal cell has nothing in this position.
ch5.plant.membrane.label: Plasma membrane, and the cytoplasm inside it
ch5.plant.membrane.do: Draw a thinner line just inside the wall, following its shape. The space inside is the cytoplasm, so leave it empty.
ch5.plant.membrane.does: The book calls this the plasma membrane. It is the real gatekeeper, selectively permeable, deciding what enters and leaves. Every living cell has one; the wall outside it is only scaffolding.
ch5.plant.nucleus.label: Nucleus
ch5.plant.nucleus.do: Draw a solid rounded blob in the upper left, about a fifth of the width.
ch5.plant.nucleus.does: Holds the instructions and decides what the cell builds. Take it out and the cell runs on for a while, then cannot replace anything.
ch5.plant.vacuole.label: Large central vacuole
ch5.plant.vacuole.do: Draw one very large rounded shape filling most of the right side.
ch5.plant.vacuole.does: A storage sac full of cell sap. In a mature plant cell it is the central vacuole, and the book says it can take up 50 to 90 per cent of the cell's volume. The sap provides turgidity and rigidity: that is what holds a soft plant upright.
ch5.plant.vacuole.only: Plant cells have one very large central vacuole. Animal cells have small ones.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.label: Chloroplasts, which are one kind of plastid
ch5.plant.chloroplast.do: Draw six green ovals scattered through the cytoplasm, tilted at different angles, and put two or three short lines inside each one.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.does: Plastids are found only in plant cells, and a plastid carrying the pigment chlorophyll is a chloroplast. Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens. The lines inside are the stacks that hold the chlorophyll.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.only: Plant cells only, and only where light reaches. Root cells have none.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.label: Mitochondria
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.do: Draw about ten small pink ovals, and run a wavy line through the middle of each. They should be smaller than the chloroplasts.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.does: Known as the powerhouses of the cell. Two membrane coverings: the outer one porous, the inner one deeply folded. That fold is also how you tell a mitochondrion from a chloroplast on a black and white exam paper, where the colours are gone.
ch5.plant.caption: A plant cell
ch5.plant.credit: Diagram after "Simple diagram of plant cell (en)" by domdomegg, CC BY 4.0
ask.ch5-u2-draw-1.order.q: Does the order matter? Could I draw the nucleus first?
ask.ch5-u2-draw-1.order.a:
You can, and your drawing will come out worse. Draw the nucleus first and you have no idea how much room to leave, so the vacuole ends up squeezed and the chloroplasts have nowhere to go.

Outside inwards is how the cell is built and how it is easiest to draw: the wall fixes the size, the membrane fixes the inside, and everything after that is placed in a space you can already see. Biologists draw it this way for the same reason you would draw a room before the furniture.
a.ch5-u2-draw-1.title: Draw a plant cell, part by part
a.ch5-u2-draw-1.blurb: Six parts, one at a time. Draw each on paper as it appears, then tap any part to ask what it does.
ch5.u2.sort.i0.label: Made of cellulose
ch5.u2.sort.i0.why: Cellulose is a plant material. Animals have none.
ch5.u2.sort.i1.label: Every living cell has one
ch5.u2.sort.i1.why: Including yours. The wall is the optional one.
ch5.u2.sort.i2.label: Decides what gets in and out
ch5.u2.sort.i3.label: Fully permeable, lets almost anything through
ch5.u2.sort.i3.why: It is scaffolding, not a filter.
ch5.u2.sort.i4.label: Stops the cell bursting in water
ch5.u2.sort.i4.why: Which is why a plant cell survives pure water and a red blood cell bursts.
ch5.u2.sort.i5.label: Present in a bacterium
ch5.u2.sort.i5.why: Bacteria have one too, though made of something other than cellulose.
a.ch5-u2-sort-2.title: Wall or membrane?
a.ch5-u2-sort-2.blurb: Two boundaries, often confused. One is alive and choosy; the other is a stiff jacket.
ch5.u3.animal.predict.prompt: You are about to draw an animal cell. Which of these will you not need?
ch5.u3.animal.predict.o2: The cell wall, the chloroplasts and the big vacuole
ch5.u3.animal.observe: Which parts did you leave out, and what changed about the shape?
ch5.u3.animal.explain: No wall, so no straight edges and no fixed shape. No chloroplasts, so it cannot make its own food. No big vacuole, so the nucleus sits near the middle instead of being pushed aside.
ch5.animal.membrane.label: Plasma membrane
ch5.animal.membrane.do: Draw one soft irregular outline. No straight edges, and no box around it.
ch5.animal.membrane.does: The plasma membrane, and the only boundary an animal cell has. This is why an animal cell has no fixed shape while a plant cell is squared off.
ch5.animal.nucleus.label: Nucleus
ch5.animal.nucleus.do: Draw a solid rounded blob, roughly in the middle this time.
ch5.animal.nucleus.does: The same job as in a plant: it holds the instructions. With no vacuole pushing it aside, it sits near the centre rather than squashed against the edge.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.label: Mitochondria
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.do: Draw nine small pink ovals scattered about, each with a wavy line through the middle.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.does: Known as the powerhouses of the cell, and with no chloroplasts in an animal cell this is where all its energy comes from. Two membrane coverings: the outer porous, the inner deeply folded.
ch5.animal.caption: An animal cell
ch5.animal.credit: Diagram after "Simple diagram of animal cell (en)" by domdomegg, CC BY 4.0
ask.ch5-u3-draw-1.shape.q: Why is the animal cell drawn wobbly and the plant cell drawn square?
ask.ch5-u3-draw-1.shape.a:
Because that is the difference the wall makes, and it is worth more than a line in a table.

A plant cell's wall is rigid, so the cell holds whatever shape the wall has, and packed together they tile like bricks. An animal cell has only its membrane, which is flexible, so it settles into whatever shape its surroundings and its own contents give it. Draw an animal cell with a ruler and you have drawn a plant cell with bits missing.
a.ch5-u3-draw-1.title: Now draw an animal cell
a.ch5-u3-draw-1.blurb: The same hand, three parts fewer. Notice what you are not drawing.
ch5.u3.sort.i0.label: Cell wall
ch5.u3.sort.i1.label: Chloroplasts
ch5.u3.sort.i1.why: Only where light reaches. Root cells have none.
ch5.u3.sort.i2.label: One large central vacuole
ch5.u3.sort.i2.why: Animal cells have small vacuoles. The book says a plant's central vacuole can be 50 to 90 per cent of the cell.
ch5.u3.sort.i3.label: Cell membrane
ch5.u3.sort.i4.label: Nucleus
ch5.u3.sort.i4.why: Both, in anything with a true nucleus.
ch5.u3.sort.i5.label: Mitochondria
ch5.u3.sort.i6.label: Centrosome
ch5.u3.sort.i6.why: Involved in cell division. Plants manage without.
a.ch5-u3-sort-2.title: Plant, animal, or both?
ch5.u4.definition: The cytoplasm is not soup with a nucleus in it. It is crowded with organelles, each doing one job: the endoplasmic reticulum moving materials about, the Golgi apparatus packaging what the cell exports, lysosomes breaking down waste, and mitochondria releasing energy. A cell is less like a bag and more like a workshop.
a.ch5-u4-read-1.title: The organelles
ch5.u4.sort.i0.label: Releases energy from food
ch5.u4.sort.i0.why: Which is why it is called the powerhouse.
ch5.u4.sort.i1.label: Packages things the cell will send out
ch5.u4.sort.i2.label: Digests worn-out parts and waste
ch5.u4.sort.i2.why: Full of digestive enzymes. The cleanup crew.
ch5.u4.sort.i3.label: Holds the instructions
ch5.u4.sort.i3.why: And controls what the cell builds.
ch5.u4.sort.i4.label: Bursts and digests the whole cell when it dies
ch5.u4.sort.i4.why: Which is why they are sometimes called suicide bags.
ch5.u4.sort.i5.label: Has its own DNA
ch5.u4.sort.i5.why: It does, which is a clue it was once a separate organism.
ask.ch5-u4-sort-2.ownDna.q: Why would the mitochondrion have its own DNA? Nothing else does.
ask.ch5-u4-sort-2.ownDna.a:
Because it was almost certainly a free-living bacterium once.

The idea is called endosymbiosis: a large cell swallowed a small one and, instead of digesting it, kept it. The evidence is hard to argue with. Mitochondria have their own DNA, in a ring like a bacterium's rather than in strands like ours. They make some of their own proteins. They divide by splitting in two, on their own schedule, not when the cell divides. And they have two membranes, which is what you would expect of something that was engulfed.

Chloroplasts have all the same features, so it seems to have happened at least twice.
a.ch5-u4-sort-2.title: Which organelle does which job?
ch5.u5.definition: Everything a cell needs has to cross its surface, and everything it uses is spread through its volume. Double the width of a cell and the surface grows four times while the volume grows eight. The bigger it gets, the less surface it has for each unit of inside to feed. That is the limit, and it is why a large organism is made of many small cells rather than a few big ones.
a.ch5-u5-read-1.title: Why no cell is large
ch5.u5.c0.prompt: A cube-shaped cell is 2 units on each side. What is its surface area? A cube has six faces.
ch5.u5.c2.prompt: Now double it: a cell 4 units on each side. Surface area divided by volume?
ch5.u5.c2.trap: The 2-unit cell scored 24 over 8, which is 3. Doubling the width halved the ratio. That is the whole argument for staying small.
a.ch5-u5-calc-2.title: Surface against volume
ch5.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: Why is a large animal made of many small cells rather than a few large ones?
ch5.u5.quiz.q0.o0: Small cells are easier to replace
ch5.u5.quiz.q0.f0: True, and not the main reason.
ch5.u5.quiz.q0.o1: A large cell has too little surface for its volume to supply it
ch5.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Right. Surface grows as the square while volume grows as the cube, so a big cell starves at the centre.
ch5.u5.quiz.q0.f2: Division speed is not what limits size.
ch5.u5.quiz.q0.f3: Some single cells are visible. An ostrich egg is one cell.
a.ch5-u5-quiz-3.title: Small for a reason
s.u1.title: Everything alive is made of cells
s.u1.blurb: One idea, arrived at by looking down a microscope at a piece of cork.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: Hooke looked at cork and called what he saw cells. What was he actually looking at?
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: The cell walls of dead cork. Everything that had been alive inside was long gone.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: "He saw cells, like the ones in us." He saw the boxes left behind, which is why he thought of monks' rooms rather than of anything living.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: Why is it useful that every living thing is made of cells?
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: One explanation covers an onion, a frog and you. A rule that broad is worth far more than a separate story for each.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: "Because they are all the same." They are not. The claim is that they are all built the same way, which is different.
s.u2.title: Draw a plant cell
s.u2.blurb: Seven parts, one at a time, and what each one is for.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Name the part that stops a plant cell bursting when it takes in water.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: "The membrane." The membrane is what lets the water in. Without the wall outside it, the cell would swell until it burst, which is exactly what a red blood cell does.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: Why is a plant's vacuole drawn so large?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Because it is. In a mature plant cell it is often most of the volume, pressing everything else against the wall.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: A small circle in a corner. Drawing it small is the commonest mistake in this diagram, and it loses the point that turgor is what holds a plant up.
recap.s.u2.q3.ask: A plant wilts. What has happened inside its cells?
recap.s.u2.q3.answer: The vacuoles have lost water, so they no longer press outwards, so the cells no longer hold each other rigid.
recap.s.u2.q3.listenFor: "The plant is dying." It may well recover in an hour with water. Wilting is mechanical before it is fatal.
s.u3.title: Draw an animal cell
s.u3.blurb: The same drawing with three things taken away. Those three are the answer to most exam questions.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Name the three things a plant cell has that an animal cell does not.
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: The cell wall, the chloroplasts, and the one large central vacuole.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Only naming the wall. The other two are worth as many marks and are forgotten twice as often.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: Why does an animal cell have no fixed shape?
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: It has only a membrane, which is flexible. Nothing holds it to a shape.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: "Because it moves around." Plenty of animal cells never move. It is the missing wall, not motion.
recap.s.u3.q3.ask: An animal cell is put in pure water and bursts. A plant cell does not. Why?
recap.s.u3.q3.answer: The wall. Both take in water and swell, but the plant cell's wall stops it expanding past a point.
recap.s.u3.q3.listenFor: "The plant cell does not take in the water." It does, and that is what makes it firm.
s.u4.title: Inside the cytoplasm
s.u4.blurb: The organelles, and the jobs they do.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Which organelle releases energy from food, and what else is odd about it?
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: The mitochondrion. It has its own DNA, in a ring, and divides on its own schedule.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: "It makes energy." It releases energy that was already in the food. Nothing makes energy.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: What does the Golgi apparatus do?
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: Receives materials, packages them, and sends them out of the cell.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: "It stores things." Storage is the vacuole. The Golgi is dispatch, not a warehouse.
recap.s.u4.q3.ask: Why are lysosomes called suicide bags?
recap.s.u4.q3.answer: They are full of digestive enzymes, and when a cell dies they burst and digest it.
recap.s.u4.q3.listenFor: "Because they kill other cells." They digest their own cell's worn-out parts, and finally the cell itself.
aid.s.u4.meaning: A garden, which is a reasonable place to keep a plant cell.
aid.s.u4.G.note: Packages what the cell sends out, and dispatches it.
aid.s.u4.D.note: Breaks down waste and worn-out parts.
aid.s.u4.N.note: Holds the instructions and decides what gets built.
s.u5.title: Why cells are small
s.u5.blurb: A question that sounds like trivia and is actually about surface area.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: Why is a large animal made of many small cells rather than a few big ones?
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: Surface grows as the square of the width while volume grows as the cube, so a large cell cannot supply its own middle.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: "Small cells are stronger." Strength is not the constraint. Supply is.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: Double a cube cell's width. What happens to its surface-to-volume ratio?
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: It halves. Surface goes up four times, volume eight.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: "It doubles" or "it stays the same". Worth working through on the board with the 2-unit and 4-unit cubes.
ask.ch5-u1-quiz-2.virus.q: Is a virus made of cells? Is it alive?
ask.ch5-u1-quiz-2.virus.a:
A virus is not made of cells, and that is exactly why nobody can agree whether it is alive.

It has genetic instructions and it can make copies of itself, which sound like life. But it has no cytoplasm, no membrane of its own making, no way to release energy and no way to build anything. It can only reproduce by getting inside a real cell and using that cell's machinery.

So the cell theory says every living thing is made of cells, and a virus sits awkwardly outside it. Most biologists resolve this by saying a virus is not alive, which is less a discovery than a decision about where to draw the line.
ask.ch5-u5-calc-2.bigcells.q: If big cells cannot work, how is an ostrich egg one cell?
ask.ch5-u5-calc-2.bigcells.a:
Because almost all of it is yolk, which is stored food rather than living, working cytoplasm.

The living part of that egg is a small disc on the surface of the yolk, and it is an ordinary size. The rule is about the part that has to be supplied across a surface, not about the total lump.

The same dodge turns up elsewhere. A nerve cell can run a metre down your leg and still obey the rule, because it is extremely thin: long in one direction only, so its surface keeps up with its volume. Cells get around the limit by changing shape, never by simply getting bigger.
ch5.plant.wall.detail.p0: Made mainly of cellulose, and lies outside the plasma membrane.
ch5.plant.wall.detail.p1: Rigid, which is what gives a plant structural strength and lets it stand without a skeleton.
ch5.plant.wall.detail.p2: Fully permeable: it lets almost anything through. The choosing is done by the membrane inside it.
ch5.plant.wall.detail.p3: It stops the cell bursting in very dilute surroundings. The cell swells, presses on the wall, and the wall presses back.
ch5.plant.wall.detail.p4: Plant cells, fungi and bacteria have one. Animal cells do not.
ch5.plant.membrane.detail.p0: The book's name for it is the plasma membrane.
ch5.plant.membrane.detail.p1: Selectively permeable: it chooses what enters and leaves, which is why the book asks you to explain that phrase.
ch5.plant.membrane.detail.p2: Every living cell has one, including yours.
ch5.plant.membrane.detail.p3: Water moves across it by osmosis, from where there is more to where there is less.
ch5.plant.membrane.detail.p4: It is flexible, which is why an animal cell has no fixed shape.
ch5.plant.nucleus.detail.p0: Holds the instructions and decides what the cell builds.
ch5.plant.nucleus.detail.p1: Wrapped in a nuclear membrane, which is double layered.
ch5.plant.nucleus.detail.p2: That membrane has pores, so material can pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
ch5.plant.nucleus.detail.p3: Inside is chromatin: a tangle of thread-like material.
ch5.plant.nucleus.detail.p4: When the cell is about to divide, the chromatin organises itself into chromosomes, which carry the DNA.
ch5.plant.nucleus.detail.p5: A cell with its nucleus removed runs on for a while and then cannot replace anything.
ch5.plant.nucleus.detail.how: A circle, a second circle just inside it, a small solid blob, and a few loose squiggles. The pores are small gaps in the outer line.
ch5.plant.vacuole.detail.p0: Storage sacs for solid or liquid contents.
ch5.plant.vacuole.detail.p1: Small in animal cells. Plant cells have very large ones.
ch5.plant.vacuole.detail.p2: The central vacuole of some plant cells may occupy 50 to 90 per cent of the cell volume.
ch5.plant.vacuole.detail.p3: In plant cells the vacuoles are full of cell sap, and provide turgidity and rigidity to the cell.
ch5.plant.vacuole.detail.p4: They store amino acids, sugars, organic acids and some proteins, and help expel excess water and some wastes.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.detail.p0: Plastids are present only in plant cells.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.detail.p1: Two types: chromoplasts, the coloured ones, and leucoplasts, the white or colourless ones, whose main job is storage.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.detail.p2: A chromoplast containing the pigment chlorophyll is a chloroplast.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.detail.p3: Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens, which is why a plant does not have to eat.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.detail.p4: The fluid inside is the stroma, and the stacks within it hold the chlorophyll.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.detail.p5: Like mitochondria, plastids carry their own DNA and ribosomes.
ch5.plant.chloroplast.detail.how: An oval with two or three short stacks of lines inside it. Do not attempt every disc.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.detail.p0: Known as the powerhouses of the cell.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.detail.p1: Two membrane coverings. The outer membrane is porous; the inner membrane is deeply folded.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.detail.p2: Those folds increase the surface area available for the reactions that generate ATP. Other books call the folds cristae; this one just calls them folds.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.detail.p3: Energy is released as ATP, adenosine triphosphate, which the book calls the energy currency of the cell.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.detail.p4: Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes, which is a clue they were once separate organisms.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.detail.p5: In a drawing, the fold is what tells one apart from a chloroplast once the colour is gone.
ch5.plant.mitochondrion.detail.how: Two ovals, one inside the other, and four or five tongues pushing in from the inner one. That is enough for full marks.
ch5.animal.membrane.detail.p0: The book's name for it is the plasma membrane.
ch5.animal.membrane.detail.p1: Selectively permeable: it chooses what enters and leaves, which is why the book asks you to explain that phrase.
ch5.animal.membrane.detail.p2: Every living cell has one, including yours.
ch5.animal.membrane.detail.p3: Water moves across it by osmosis, from where there is more to where there is less.
ch5.animal.membrane.detail.p4: It is flexible, which is why an animal cell has no fixed shape.
ch5.animal.nucleus.detail.p0: Holds the instructions and decides what the cell builds.
ch5.animal.nucleus.detail.p1: Wrapped in a nuclear membrane, which is double layered.
ch5.animal.nucleus.detail.p2: That membrane has pores, so material can pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
ch5.animal.nucleus.detail.p3: Inside is chromatin: a tangle of thread-like material.
ch5.animal.nucleus.detail.p4: When the cell is about to divide, the chromatin organises itself into chromosomes, which carry the DNA.
ch5.animal.nucleus.detail.p5: A cell with its nucleus removed runs on for a while and then cannot replace anything.
ch5.animal.nucleus.detail.how: A circle, a second circle just inside it, a small solid blob, and a few loose squiggles. The pores are small gaps in the outer line.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.detail.p0: Releases energy from food, which the cell then spends on everything else. The book calls it the powerhouse of the cell.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.detail.p1: Two membranes, not one. The outer is smooth; the inner is folded.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.detail.p2: Those folds are called cristae. They pack a large surface into a small space, and the energy-releasing reactions happen on that surface.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.detail.p3: The fluid inside the folds is the matrix.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.detail.p4: It has its own DNA, in a ring like a bacterium's, and divides on its own schedule.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.detail.p5: In a drawing, the fold is what tells it apart from a chloroplast once the colour is gone.
ch5.animal.mitochondrion.detail.how: Two ovals, one inside the other, and four or five tongues pushing in from the inner one. That is enough for full marks.
ch5.plant.vacuole.detail.p5: In a single-celled organism like Amoeba, the food vacuole holds the food it has taken in.
